theme: Jerusalem populated; the wall dedicated; final reforms
readingInstruction: Read Nehemiah 11:1-13:31. The city is repopulated and the wall is dedicated with two great choirs. Then Nehemiah returns from a trip to Susa and finds that the people have already slipped back into old sins. Notice the ending.
settingTheScene: Chapter 11 lists those who settled in Jerusalem, chosen by lot to bring one in ten from the towns. Chapter 12 describes the joyful dedication of the wall. Chapter 13 jumps ahead, probably about 432 BC. Nehemiah had returned to Persia for a time. When he comes back, he finds that Tobiah has been given a room in the temple, the Levites are unpaid, the Sabbath is being broken, and some have married foreign wives again.
observation: “And the people blessed all the men who willingly offered to live in Jerusalem” (11:2).
“And at the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem they sought the Levites… to celebrate the dedication with gladness” (12:27).
“And I brought the leaders of Judah up onto the wall, and appointed two great choirs that gave thanks” (12:31).
“And they offered great sacrifices that day and rejoiced, for God had made them rejoice with great joy” (12:43).
“And the sound of the joy of Jerusalem was heard far away” (12:43).
“And I was very angry, and I threw all the household furniture of Tobiah out of the chamber” (13:8).
“Why is the house of God forsaken?” (13:11).
“Remember me, O my God, for good” (13:31).
interpretation:
The dedication of the wall is a high point. Two great choirs and processions go around the wall in opposite directions, singing, with cymbals, harps, and lyres, and meet at the temple. The people offer sacrifices, and “God had made them rejoice with great joy.” Women and children rejoice too. The sound of Jerusalem’s joy is heard far away. This recalls the sound at the foundation of the temple in Ezra 3, but now it is clearly joy, without the weeping.

And then chapter 13 is a sober coda. Nehemiah returns and finds the covenant broken. Tobiah, the enemy who had mocked the builders, now lives in a storeroom of the temple. The Levites have gone back to their farms because no one paid them. The Sabbath markets are in full swing. Some have married foreign wives. Nehemiah’s reaction is fierce. He throws out Tobiah’s furniture, restores the tithes, shuts the gates on the Sabbath, and rebukes those who intermarried.

The lesson is plain. Reform does not last on its own. A wall can be built in fifty-two days, a covenant can be signed in a day, but the human heart drifts back. Even after confession and revival, the people forgot. This is why the Old Testament ends not with triumph but with a longing for something deeper. The law written on stone and walls built of stone cannot change the heart.

Nehemiah ends with a prayer: “Remember me, O my God, for good.” It is the prayer of a faithful servant who knows that his work is not finished. The book closes with unresolved tension: God’s people are back, but they need a better covenant. The new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 is still ahead.
connection: Jeremiah 31:33 promises a law written on the heart. Hebrews 8:6-13 says Jesus mediates a better covenant. Ezekiel 36:26: “I will give you a new heart.” Galatians 3:3 asks, “Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?” Revelation 2:4 warns about leaving our first love. 1 Corinthians 10:12: “Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.”
application:
Think about a reform in your life that has slipped. What helps a good change last?

Be humble about your own heart. Ask a trusted friend to check on you in an area of past failure.

Thank God that the new covenant does not depend on our consistency but on Christ.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the joy of those who worship him.
Ask him to keep you from drifting back.
Ask him to write his law on your heart.
